title: Racing for a good cause
text: It is three in the morning, and more than one hundred thousand people are watching a young woman try to finish a video game from the nineties in under an hour. Behind her, a small crowd is cheering, and in a corner of the screen a number keeps rising: the amount of money that viewers have donated to charity. This is Games Done Quick, a week-long marathon of speedruns that takes place twice a year and has become one of the most unusual fundraising events in the world.

The idea started in a surprisingly modest way. In 2010, a group of speedrunners met in a basement in the United States and streamed their runs online, asking viewers to donate to a charity. They hoped to raise a few thousand dollars. Instead, they collected over ten thousand. Encouraged by this success, they organised another event, and then another. Today the marathons are held in large hotel conference rooms, the runs are broadcast without a break for seven days, and the total raised over the years has reached tens of millions of dollars.

Each marathon supports a different cause. The winter event, held in January, raises money for an organisation that fights cancer, while the summer event supports Doctors Without Borders, which provides medical care in war zones and areas hit by disasters. For many viewers, this is what makes the marathons special. They are not only watching incredible skill; they are also helping people they will never meet.

The organisers have found creative ways to encourage donations. Viewers can pay to choose the name of a character, vote on which path a runner should take or unlock an extra challenge, such as completing a level with their eyes closed. Runners often explain the tricks they are using as they play, so even people who know nothing about the game can follow what is happening. The atmosphere is friendly and enthusiastic, and mistakes are greeted with sympathy rather than criticism.

Behind the scenes, the event requires an enormous amount of preparation. Hundreds of runners apply to take part, and a selection committee watches their videos to decide who will appear. Every run must be entertaining, reliable and safe for a general audience. Volunteers work in shifts to control the cameras, read out donation messages and keep the schedule on time, which is no easy task when a single unexpected glitch can make a run last twenty minutes longer than planned.

Not every runner finds the experience easy. Performing a run in front of a live audience is very different from practising alone at home, and even experienced players admit that their hands shake when they sit down. Yet most of them say the pressure is worth it. For a community that is often seen as strange or antisocial, the marathons are a chance to show what gamers can do when they work together.

Perhaps that is the real secret of their success. Speedrunning is usually about individuals racing against the clock. At Games Done Quick, however, the most important number on the screen is not the time, but the total at the bottom: proof that a hobby can make a real difference.
